newsitem.title: KUWAIT: FEATURE - Kuwaiti women to strike for political rights.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kuwaiti women to strike for political rights.

text.p: Kuwaiti women run businesses, head diplomatic missions and help to steer the country's oil industry but when Kuwaitis go to the polls on October 7, they won't take part.
Women are barred from running for parliament or even voting.
Activists for women's rights have renewed their 30-year campaign for what some -- including Moslem traditionalists -- see as a right guaranteed by Kuwait's constitution and Islam.
They have called on women to stay home from work on Sunday in a demand for political rights.
"Why don't you, citizen sister, express your objection to discrimination practised against you? Join us in the work strike day," the activists said in a statement.
Campaigners have had to fight on two fronts -- to lobby men for the right to vote while persuading women to back their struggle.
"A woman should stay home and raise children," said one angry bedouin of demands by Kuwaiti women for political rights.

Denying women the right to vote is among the few things that unite Kuwaiti politicians -- for now at least. Many liberals are concerned that if women were allowed to vote, Islamists would increase their strength in parliament.
They say Moslem traditionalists are better organised and women would vote for candidates picked by the man in the house.
"Women in Britain, for instance, were not given the right to vote until decades of democracy had passed," said liberal parliament member Abdul-Mohsen al-Mudej, a former oil minister.
Western powers which helped liberate Kuwait in 1991 of an Iraqi occupation have praised democratic reforms introduced in Kuwait while urging the country to give women the right to vote.
"It is unfinished business," said a senior Western diplomat.
During the Iraqi occupation the Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah said in exile he would consider allowing women to vote, adding that the issue required time.
The debate was revived in 1992 when Kuwait's parliament was restored but both the assembly and the government appeared reluctant to introduce the reform.
Women activists have held sporadic protests in Kuwait to demand political rights. In March about 40 woman lawyers, scientists and academics demonstrated outside parliament.

Mona al-Ghareeb, a woman consultant at parliament and a university teacher who plans to join the strike on Sunday, told Reuters: "Political awarness among men was less in the past, now they are better. This is also true for women."

Women now accept that they will not take part in the vote for the parliament which will take Kuwait into the next century but they are trying to woo candidates to support their cause in the new assembly.
Few believe a post-election cabinet would include a woman, unprecedented in Gulf Arab states.
"Women's campaign to change their social and political situation will not pay if change was anticipated from the powers of darkness (hardline deputies)," wrote liberal columnist Naji al-Zaid.
"They have only one way: urge the Emir," he wrote in al-Qabas newspaper.
